label: Annular and figurate lesions
lead: Annularity is a configuration, not a diagnosis — but it narrows the field sharply. The discriminating question is what the edge is doing: a scaly advancing edge means the organism is in the stratum corneum and a KOH will find it; a smooth beaded edge with no scale means the process is dermal and needs a biopsy.

stop.l: Expanding annular lesion after travel or tick exposure, with fever or facial palsy
stop.a: Disseminated Lyme borreliosis. Serology and treat empirically — do not wait. Neurologic and cardiac involvement follow if untreated.

stop.l: Annular plaques with anesthesia within the lesion
stop.a: Leprosy. Test light touch, pinprick and temperature inside the patch, palpate the peripheral nerves, and refer to a leprosy service. Notifiable in most jurisdictions.
Erythema multiforme major or SJS. Look at the mouth, eyes and genitals before you settle on an annular label.

stop.l: Rapidly expanding annular erythema with fever and a new murmur
stop.a: Erythema marginatum of acute rheumatic fever. ASO titer, ECG and echocardiography.

stop.l: Migratory erosive annular erythema with weight loss and new diabetes
stop.a: Consider necrolytic migratory erythema and the glucagonoma syndrome. Check a fasting serum glucagon and glucose and image the pancreas.

dx.look: Red-brown to violaceous papules and annular or infiltrated plaques, classically on the face and around the eyes and nose, with an apple-jelly color on diascopy; a great mimic that imitates granuloma annulare, lupus and lymphoma. Lupus pernio (violaceous nose and cheek plaques) signals chronic systemic disease.
fr: Red-brown papules or plaques with an apple-jelly color on diascopy
Annular or infiltrated plaques, often on the face
Involvement of scars and tattoos
Lupus pernio on the nose (chronic systemic disease)
Systemic features - hilar adenopathy, uveitis, arthralgia
ag: Prominent epidermal scale (sarcoid is usually a dermal process)
A single self-limited ring in a young adult
dx.cf: Biopsy shows non-caseating (naked) granulomas; then screen for systemic disease - chest imaging, serum ACE, calcium, an eye exam and pulmonary and cardiac assessment.
dx.dsc: Orange-yellow structureless areas (apple-jelly) with focal linear or branching vessels - a granulomatous pattern shared with other granulomas.
dx.hp: Superficial and deep dermal collections of epithelioid histiocytes forming non-caseating (naked) granulomas with sparse surrounding lymphocytes; stains and cultures are negative for organisms.
dx.assoc: A cutaneous sign of a multisystem disease - screen with chest imaging, serum ACE and calcium, an eye exam and pulmonary and cardiac assessment. Lupus pernio predicts chronic systemic involvement.
dx.mgmt: Localized disease - potent topical or intralesional corticosteroids; widespread or disfiguring disease - hydroxychloroquine, methotrexate or a TNF inhibitor; treat systemic disease per organ involvement.

dx.look: Migratory annular and polycyclic erythema with superficial flaccid blisters, erosions and crusting, favoring the perineum, groin, buttocks and perioral skin; it waxes and wanes and heals with hyperpigmentation, and is the cutaneous marker of a glucagon-secreting pancreatic tumor (glucagonoma syndrome).
fr: Migratory annular erythema with superficial erosion and crusting
Perineal, groin, buttock and perioral distribution
Angular cheilitis, glossitis, weight loss and diabetes
A waxing-and-waning course with hyperpigmented healing
Flaccid blistering at the advancing edge
ag: A purely scaly plaque without erosion
dx.cf: Check a fasting serum glucagon (markedly elevated) and glucose and image the pancreas; also consider glucagonoma-independent causes (cirrhosis, malabsorption, zinc or amino-acid deficiency).
dx.hp: Psoriasiform hyperplasia with characteristic upper-epidermal pallor and necrosis of the stratum spinosum (necrolysis) and confluent parakeratosis.
dx.assoc: The skin marker of glucagonoma syndrome - check serum glucagon, glucose, zinc and amino acids and image the pancreas; also seen with cirrhosis and malabsorption (pseudoglucagonoma).
dx.mgmt: Treat the underlying tumor (resection) or deficiency; correct amino-acid, zinc and fatty-acid deficits; somatostatin analogs and supportive skin care for the eruption.

dx.look: Annular or polycyclic plaque with a raised, scaly, sometimes pustular advancing edge and central clearing. Asymmetric, usually few. Look for the reservoir: feet, groin, nails, or an animal.
fr: Scale concentrated at the advancing edge
Central clearing
Asymmetric, one or few lesions
Concurrent tinea pedis, cruris or onychomycosis
Worsened by topical steroid
ag: No scale anywhere on the lesion
dx.cf: KOH from the scaly edge. Culture when KOH is negative or before systemic therapy.
dx.dsc: Peripheral white scale on the advancing edge with broken or bent hairs where vellus hair is involved; the background is otherwise nonspecific.
dx.hp: PAS-positive septate hyphae confined to the stratum corneum (the sandwich sign) over a mildly spongiotic epidermis.
dx.assoc: Hunt for the reservoir - tinea pedis, cruris or onychomycosis - and for zoophilic contact; consider immunosuppression when widespread.
dx.mgmt: Topical azole or terbinafine for localized disease; oral terbinafine or itraconazole when extensive, follicular, or steroid-modified.

dx.look: Firm, smooth, skin-colored to violaceous dermal papules in an annular arrangement with a beaded border and a depressed, normal-textured center. No scale at all. Dorsal hands and feet, and over joints. Asymptomatic.
fr: Complete absence of scale
Firm beaded border of discrete papules
Dorsa of hands and feet, over joints
Asymptomatic — the patient noticed it, it did not bother them
Skin-colored or violaceous rather than red
ag: Central clearing with erythema rather than normal skin
dx.cf: The absence of scale is the diagnosis. Diascopy may show apple-jelly change. Biopsy shows palisading granulomas around mucin. Check glucose in generalized disease.
dx.dsc: A whitish-orange structureless background with fine dotted or short linear vessels and no epidermal scale (which helps separate it from tinea).
dx.hp: Palisading histiocytes around foci of degenerated collagen with mucin (necrobiosis) in the dermis - an interstitial or palisaded granulomatous pattern.
dx.assoc: Usually idiopathic and self-limited; the disseminated form has a debated association with diabetes and dyslipidemia - check glucose and lipids if widespread.
dx.mgmt: Reassurance (often self-resolving); potent topical or intralesional corticosteroids for localized disease; phototherapy or systemic agents for disseminated disease.
dx.pat: Dorsal hands and feet, over joints

dx.look: An expanding erythematous patch appearing 3–30 days after a tick bite, enlarging to over 5 cm, often with central clearing giving a bull's-eye. Warm but not usually painful or itchy. Flu-like symptoms may accompany it.
fr: Endemic exposure and outdoor activity
Expanding steadily over days to weeks
Larger than 5 cm
Little or no scale
Flu-like symptoms, arthralgia
dx.cf: In an endemic area, a typical expanding lesion over 5 cm is diagnostic clinically and should be treated without serology — antibodies are frequently negative this early. Serology is for later-stage disease.
dx.hp: A superficial and deep perivascular lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate, sometimes with eosinophils; spirochetes are difficult to demonstrate.
dx.assoc: An expanding annular erythema at a tick-bite site (Borrelia); it may be multiple. Watch for early disseminated disease - carditis, neuritis, arthritis.
dx.mgmt: Oral doxycycline first-line (amoxicillin or cefuroxime in children and pregnancy); in an endemic exposure, treat clinically without waiting for serology.

dx.look: Slowly migrating annular and polycyclic erythema with a characteristic trailing scale that lies just inside the advancing edge. Trunk and proximal limbs. Persists for months, waxing and waning. A reaction pattern to infection, drug or, rarely, malignancy.
fr: Trailing scale inside the advancing border
Slow centrifugal migration over weeks
Trunk and proximal limbs
Recurrent over months
dx.cf: Biopsy shows a tight perivascular lymphocytic coat-sleeve infiltrate. Search for a trigger: dermatophyte infection elsewhere, drug, and in older patients consider an underlying malignancy.
dx.dsc: Trailing scale inside an erythematous advancing edge, with nonspecific vessels.
dx.hp: A tight coat-sleeve perivascular lymphocytic cuffing in the dermis, with focal parakeratosis in the superficial (scaling) variant.
dx.assoc: A reactive figurate erythema - search for a trigger (dermatophyte, drug, viral infection, rarely malignancy) and treat the underlying cause.
dx.mgmt: Identify and treat the trigger; topical corticosteroids for symptom relief. It waxes and wanes over months.

dx.look: Plaques clearing centrally while the edge remains sharply marginated and silvery-scaled. Usually accompanied by more typical psoriasis elsewhere, and by nail change.
fr: Sharp margin with silvery scale over the whole ring
Typical psoriatic plaques elsewhere
Nail pitting or oil-drop sign
Symmetric extensor involvement
ag: Scale only at the leading edge
dx.cf: Look at the nails, scalp, umbilicus and natal cleft — the diagnosis is usually made somewhere other than the lesion in question.
dx.dsc: Regularly distributed dotted (glomerular) vessels over a light-red background with diffuse white scale; the uniformity of the vessel pattern is the dermoscopic hallmark.
dx.hp: Confluent parakeratosis with Munro microabscesses, regular psoriasiform acanthosis with thinned suprapapillary plates, and dilated tortuous capillaries in the dermal papillae.
dx.assoc: Psoriatic arthritis in up to a third, plus metabolic syndrome and cardiovascular disease - ask about joint symptoms and screen cardiometabolic risk. Guttate flares follow streptococcal pharyngitis.
dx.mgmt: Localized disease - a topical vitamin D analog (calcipotriene) with a topical corticosteroid; extensive disease - narrowband UVB, then methotrexate, acitretin, cyclosporine, or a biologic.

dx.look: Photodistributed annular-polycyclic plaques with a fine peripheral scale on the upper back, shoulders, V of the neck and extensor arms, sparing the knuckles and the sun-shadowed areas. Non-scarring, heals with hypopigmentation. Anti-Ro/SSA positive.
fr: Strict photodistribution
Sparing of sun-shadowed sites and knuckles
Heals with hypopigmentation, not scarring
Recent hydrochlorothiazide, terbinafine, PPI or TNF inhibitor
dx.cf: Biopsy with direct immunofluorescence, ANA, anti-Ro/SSA and anti-La/SSB. Read the drug list — drug-induced SCLE is identical and only the history finds it.
dx.hp: Interface (vacuolar) dermatitis with dermal mucin and a superficial perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate; direct immunofluorescence shows a granular lupus band.
dx.assoc: Anti-Ro/SSA positive in the majority - check ANA, anti-Ro and anti-La; review drugs (hydrochlorothiazide, terbinafine, PPIs, TNF inhibitors) and assess for systemic lupus.
dx.mgmt: Strict photoprotection, a topical corticosteroid or calcineurin inhibitor, and hydroxychloroquine first-line; stop any culprit drug.

dx.look: At the site of a sandfly bite, weeks to months earlier: a papule enlarging to a nodule and then to a shallow ulcer with a raised, indurated, rolled border and an adherent crust. Exposed sites — face, arms, legs. Painless. Slow, indolent evolution over months.
fr: Residence in or travel to an endemic area
Exposed site: face, forearm, lower leg
Painless, indolent, present for months
Raised indurated rolled border
Satellite papules or a nodular lymphangitic chain
dx.cf: Slit-skin smear from the indurated edge with Giemsa staining to show amastigotes, plus PCR for speciation — species determines whether systemic therapy is needed. Culture on NNN medium where available.
dx.dsc: Yellow tears and central erosion with peripheral hairpin or comma vessels and white starburst-like structures over an erythematous background.
dx.hp: A granulomatous dermal infiltrate with amastigotes inside macrophages (parasites lining the histiocyte membrane - the marquee sign).
dx.assoc: Travel or residence in an endemic area with a chronic non-healing papule or ulcer; confirm by smear, PCR (which also speciates), or culture. Consider mucosal risk with New-World species.
dx.mgmt: Species- and severity-dependent - local therapy (cryotherapy, intralesional antimony, thermotherapy) for simple Old-World lesions; systemic antimonials, liposomal amphotericin B or miltefosine for complex or mucosal disease.

dx.look: Coin-shaped, intensely itchy, weeping or crusted plaques on a background of xerosis. May appear ring-like when the center dries first, but the scale is spread over the whole lesion rather than concentrated at the edge.
fr: Intense itch
Scale and crust across the whole plaque
Background xerosis
Multiple similar lesions on extensor legs
ag: True central clearing to normal skin
dx.cf: KOH first — it is the lesion most often mistaken for tinea and vice versa.
dx.dsc: Patchy dotted vessels with yellowish serocrust in a nonspecific eczematous pattern; used mainly to help exclude tinea.
dx.hp: Spongiotic dermatitis with acanthosis and a serum-scale crust; biopsy serves to exclude tinea or mycosis fungoides.
dx.assoc: Background xerosis and atopy; patch test refractory cases and exclude tinea with KOH.
dx.mgmt: Liberal emollients with a mid- to high-potency topical corticosteroid; treat secondary infection and correct the dry skin.

dx.look: One to three well-demarcated waxy plaques on the shin, with a slightly raised brownish-red border and a depressed yellow-orange atrophic center crossed by prominent telangiectasia. Larger lesions merge centrifugally into serpiginous or polycyclic shapes. Ulceration is common and heals with depressed scars.
fr: Yellow-orange depressed center with visible telangiectasia
Pretibial - more than 80 percent occur on the shin
Raised brownish-red advancing border
Epidermal atrophy so the surface looks like waxed paper
Known diabetes or impaired glucose tolerance
Ulceration after minor trauma
ag: Firm beaded border of discrete papules over a normal-textured center
dx.cf: The waxy yellow atrophic center with telangiectasia on a shin is the diagnosis. Biopsy the active border only when granuloma annulare, sarcoidosis or xanthoma need excluding, and check fasting glucose or HbA1c.
dx.dsc: Coarse branching serpentine vessels over a yellow-orange structureless background with white fibrotic streaks - the yellow is deeper and the vessels far coarser than in granuloma annulare.
dx.hp: Sclerosis with loss of the normal collagen bundle pattern (necrobiosis) in the lower dermis, surrounded by horizontally arranged palisaded granulomatous inflammation, with microangiopathy.
dx.assoc: About a third have clinical diabetes, a third have abnormal glucose tolerance alone and a third are normoglycemic, so check fasting glucose or HbA1c in everyone. Severity does not track diabetic control, and tightening control does not alter the course.
dx.mgmt: Potent topical corticosteroid, or intralesional triamcinolone into the active border, arrests extension. Do not occlude an ulcerated lesion - occlusion itself provokes ulceration. Most ulcers heal with local wound care; excision with grafting is reserved for the rest.

dx.look: Dull-red targets: a 1 to 2 cm papule that acquires concentric zones - a dusky or vesicular center, a pale edematous ring, an erythematous rim. Acral and symmetric, favoring dorsal hands, palms, soles, forearms, elbows and knees. Crops evolve over about 10 days and each individual lesion stays where it is.
fr: Three-zoned target with a dusky or blistered center
Symmetric acral distribution - dorsal hands, palms, soles, elbows, knees
Herpes labialis in the preceding 1 to 2 weeks
Crops over about 10 days with individual lesions fixed in place
Erosions of lips, mouth, conjunctiva or genitals in the major form
ag: Scale concentrated at the advancing edge
dx.cf: Clinical. Look in the mouth, at the eyes and at the genitals before settling on the label - mucosal involvement defines erythema multiforme major and changes the disposition. Take a history of herpes labialis, Mycoplasma infection and new drugs; biopsy only when Stevens-Johnson syndrome or another interface disease is in play.
dx.hp: Interface dermatitis with apoptotic keratinocytes and focal epidermal necrosis, papillary dermal edema and a perivascular mononuclear infiltrate; subepidermal blistering in severe lesions, and full-thickness necrosis in the most severe.
dx.assoc: Most cases follow herpes simplex; Mycoplasma pneumoniae and drugs (sulfonamides, phenytoin, barbiturates, penicillin, allopurinol) account for much of the rest. Recurrent disease is HSV-driven even when no cold sore is recalled.
dx.mgmt: The minor form is self-limited - symptomatic care, a topical corticosteroid, and an oral antiviral if herpes is active. The major form needs mucosal care, ophthalmology review and admission if oral intake fails. Prevent recurrent disease with continuous suppressive valacyclovir or acyclovir.

dx.look: One to a few sharply defined, raised annular plaques with an erythematous or purple border and a hypopigmented, dry, atrophic center, enlarging peripherally over months to years. The lesion is anesthetic and devoid of sweat glands and hair. A thickened nerve may be palpable at the edge, and the ulnar, great auricular, peroneal or posterior tibial trunks are often enlarged.
fr: Reduced light touch, pinprick or temperature inside the patch
Thickened nerve at the edge of the lesion, or an enlarged peripheral nerve trunk
Loss of hair and sweating within the plaque
Sharply defined raised border with a hypopigmented, atrophic center
Birth in or long residence in an endemic country
Few asymmetric lesions, present for months to years
dx.cf: Test light touch, pinprick and temperature inside the patch against adjacent normal skin, palpate the ulnar, great auricular, peroneal and posterior tibial nerves, and take a slit-skin smear with a skin biopsy for acid-fast bacilli. The diagnosis is made on any one cardinal finding: characteristic lesions with sensory loss, enlarged peripheral nerves, or demonstration of M. leprae. Notifiable in most jurisdictions.
dx.hp: Epithelioid cell granulomas forming around dermal nerves, with sparse or absent acid-fast bacilli in tuberculoid and borderline tuberculoid disease; PCR detects M. leprae DNA when the bacterial index is negative.
dx.assoc: Nerve damage drives the morbidity - claw hand, foot drop, plantar ulceration, lagophthalmos and corneal insensitivity. Type 1 (reversal) reactions cause acute nerve inflammation with sudden loss of function and are a neurologic emergency. Squamous cell carcinoma arises in chronic neurotrophic ulcers. Screen household contacts.
dx.mgmt: WHO multidrug therapy through a leprosy service - rifampin, dapsone and clofazimine for everyone, 6 months for paucibacillary and 12 months for multibacillary disease (the uniform three-drug regimen has replaced two-drug therapy for paucibacillary disease). Treat reactions promptly with prednisone to save nerve function, and start education and protective care of the anesthetic hand and foot on day one.
dx.pat: Few asymmetric plaques, cool exposed sites

dx.look: Sharply defined coppery to brownish-red annular and polycyclic plaques, characteristically merging on the face in people with darker skin, alongside firm keratotic papules on the palms and soles. Lesions are scattered, discrete, symmetric and asymptomatic. Arciform lesions mark relapsing disease.
fr: Coppery, ham-colored annular plaques, often on the face
Firm scaling papules on the palms and soles
Asymptomatic despite widespread lesions
Mucous patches, condylomata lata or moth-eaten alopecia
Fever, sore throat, weight loss and generalized lymphadenopathy
A new sexual partner, or a healed painless genital ulcer
ag: A single ring with no lesions anywhere else
A firm beaded dermal border with no scale at all
dx.cf: RPR or VDRL with a confirmatory treponemal test (TPPA or FTA-ABS). Serology is essentially always reactive in secondary syphilis, so a negative RPR against a compatible picture should prompt a request for serial dilution to exclude the prozone effect. Test for HIV and other sexually transmitted infections at the same visit.
dx.hp: Lymphocytic and plasmacytic dermal infiltrate with proliferation of capillaries and lymphatics and endarteritis; a Dieterle or Warthin-Starry stain or an immunostain demonstrates spirochetes.
dx.assoc: The great imitator, and a systemic infection - fever, sore throat, weight loss, headache and meningismus travel with it. Test for HIV, screen for other sexually transmitted infections, and trace and treat partners. Notifiable.
dx.mgmt: Intramuscular benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units - a single dose treats early syphilis. Refer penicillin-allergic patients to an infectious disease specialist rather than substituting an oral agent on your own. Warn about the Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction and follow non-treponemal titers to confirm response.

dx.look: Concentric migrating bands of erythema with a fine trailing scale, arranged in a wood-grain or knotty-pine pattern across the trunk and proximal limbs. It moves fast enough - up to about a centimeter a day - that the pattern visibly changes between visits. Itch is usually marked.
fr: Concentric wood-grain or knotty-pine whorls
Visible migration from one day to the next
Trailing scale on the inner side of the bands
Widespread truncal involvement in an adult over 50
Weight loss, anemia or another constitutional change
dx.cf: The pattern is the diagnosis; histology is nonspecific. The finding obliges a search for an internal malignancy - lung, esophagus and breast are the usual culprits - with history, examination, chest imaging, cross-sectional imaging and age-appropriate cancer screening. The eruption clears when the tumor is treated.
dx.hp: Nonspecific - mild spongiosis with focal parakeratosis and a superficial perivascular lymphohistiocytic infiltrate; direct immunofluorescence is usually negative.
dx.assoc: A paraneoplastic figurate erythema listed among the mucocutaneous signs of systemic cancer. The great majority of reported cases have an underlying carcinoma, most often bronchial. Treat the tumor and the rash follows.
dx.mgmt: Find and treat the malignancy - that is the treatment. Topical corticosteroids and antihistamines control the itch meanwhile, and the eruption resolves once the tumor is removed.

dx.n: Erythema marginatum of acute rheumatic fever
dx.s: Fitzpatrick 8e §8 Table 8-2; revised Jones criteria for acute rheumatic fever
dx.look: Evanescent flat or slightly raised pink rings and arcs with a well-defined serpiginous outer edge and a pale center, on the trunk and proximal limbs and never on the face. Individual lesions appear and vanish within hours and are brought out by heat. Non-pruritic and non-scaling.
fr: Rings appear and disappear within hours, changing shape while you watch
Trunk and proximal limbs, sparing the face
No scale and no itch
Fever, migratory polyarthritis, chorea or a new murmur
Streptococcal pharyngitis 2 to 5 weeks earlier
Child or adolescent
ag: A fixed ring persisting for weeks
An adult with no infectious prodrome
dx.cf: Document preceding group A streptococcal infection with an ASO or anti-DNase B titer or throat culture, then apply the revised Jones criteria. Get an ECG for PR prolongation and an echocardiogram for carditis. Erythema marginatum is a major Jones criterion and is missed because the rings come and go between examinations.
dx.hp: Nonspecific - a sparse perivascular and interstitial neutrophilic and lymphocytic infiltrate in the upper dermis. Biopsy is rarely done and rarely helps.
dx.assoc: A major manifestation of acute rheumatic fever, traveling with carditis, migratory polyarthritis, chorea and subcutaneous nodules. The valve, not the skin, is what matters.
dx.mgmt: Treat the streptococcal infection with penicillin, manage the rheumatic fever with anti-inflammatory therapy and cardiology assessment, and start long-term secondary antibiotic prophylaxis. The rash itself needs nothing.
dx.pat: Trunk and proximal limbs, sparing face

ctx.l: Endemic area for leishmaniasis (Middle East, North Africa, Central Asia, Latin America)
ctx.s: Cutaneous leishmaniasis is endemic across the Arabian peninsula, Fitzpatrick 8e §29

ctx.l: Tick exposure or travel to a Lyme-endemic region

ctx.s: Association reported with generalized granuloma annulare, Fitzpatrick 8e §15

ctx.l: New drug in the last 8 weeks
Treated with topical steroid and it spread

ctx.s: Most erythema multiforme is HSV-driven, Fitzpatrick 8e §14

ctx.l: Born in or long residence in a leprosy-endemic country (South Asia, Brazil, Indonesia, sub-Saharan Africa)
New sexual partner or another sexually transmitted infection in the last year
Sore throat 2 to 5 weeks ago, now with fever and migratory joint pain
ctx.s: Revised Jones criteria for acute rheumatic fever; post-streptococcal guttate psoriasis is the other consequence

find.l: Scale concentrated at the advancing edge
Trailing scale lying just inside the advancing border
No scale anywhere on the lesion
Firm dermal papules forming a beaded border
Completely asymptomatic — no itch, no pain
Expanded steadily to more than 5 cm over days to weeks
Strictly photodistributed
Central ulceration with a raised indurated rolled border
Present for months with very slow change
find.s: Indolence is characteristic of leishmaniasis and granuloma annulare

find.l: Reduced sensation within the lesion
find.s: Anesthesia within an annular plaque should trigger evaluation for leprosy regardless of the ranking below, Fitzpatrick 8e §25

find.l: Typical psoriasis or nail change elsewhere
Intense pruritus with weeping or crusting
Concurrent tinea pedis, cruris or onychomycosis
Apple-jelly color on diascopy of a red-brown infiltrated plaque
Migratory erosive annular erythema of the groin and perioral skin with weight loss
Waxy yellow-orange atrophic center with prominent telangiectasia on the shin
Ulceration arising inside an established plaque on the lower leg
Three-zoned target with a dusky or blistered center
Symmetric acral distribution - dorsal hands, palms, soles, elbows and knees
Herpes labialis in the 1 to 2 weeks before the eruption
Thickened nerve palpable at the edge of the lesion, or an enlarged peripheral nerve trunk
Loss of hair and sweating within the plaque
Coppery annular plaques on the face with firm scaling papules on palms and soles
Mucous patches, condylomata lata, moth-eaten alopecia or generalized lymphadenopathy
Concentric wood-grain whorls that visibly migrate from one day to the next
Weight loss, anemia or another constitutional change in an adult over 50
find.s: A figurate erythema in an older adult warrants a malignancy search, Fitzpatrick 8e §19

find.l: Rings appear and disappear within hours, with fever and migratory joint pain
find.s: Revised Jones criteria for acute rheumatic fever; Fitzpatrick 8e §8 Table 8-2

find.l: Annular polycyclic plaques resolving with hypopigmentation and telangiectasia but no scarring
find.s: Fitzpatrick 8e §14 - subacute cutaneous lupus heals with hypopigmentation, not scarring

find.l: Red-brown papules arising inside an old scar or a tattoo

test.l: Biopsy for non-caseating granulomas plus a systemic screen
test.w: Red-brown infiltrated papules or plaques with apple-jelly diascopy, or any granulomatous facial eruption.
test.p: Non-caseating naked granulomas support sarcoidosis. Then screen systemically - chest imaging, ACE, calcium and an eye exam.
test.n: Granulomas are nonspecific - stains and cultures must exclude infection (mycobacteria, fungi) before committing.
test.x: Always stain and culture a granuloma; infection is the great mimic of cutaneous sarcoidosis.

test.l: KOH from the scaly advancing edge
test.w: Every annular scaly lesion, before any steroid.
test.n: Does not exclude pretreated tinea. Culture or repeat after two weeks off treatment.
test.x: Scrape the edge, not the center. The center of a treated ring is often sterile while the edge is teeming.

test.w: A non-scaly annular lesion with a firm beaded border, when the patient wants a name or when the lesion is generalized.
test.p: Palisading histiocytes around degenerated collagen and mucin confirms granuloma annulare. Check glucose in generalized disease.
test.n: Consider necrobiosis lipoidica, sarcoidosis and annular elastolytic giant cell granuloma as the alternatives.
test.x: Granuloma annulare is frequently treated for months as tinea because nobody scraped it and nobody noticed the lack of scale.

test.l: Slit-skin smear with Giemsa, plus PCR for speciation
test.w: Any chronic, painless, indolent ulcerated nodule with a raised border in a patient from or returning from an endemic area.
test.p: Amastigotes within macrophages confirm it. PCR speciation matters: Old World cutaneous disease is often managed locally, while species with mucosal potential require systemic therapy.
test.n: Smear sensitivity falls as lesions age and organisms become scanty. A negative smear with a compatible history and morphology warrants PCR or biopsy.
test.x: Sample from the indurated edge, not the ulcer floor — the floor yields necrotic debris and contaminating bacteria. Clean and de-crust first.

test.l: Serology for Borrelia (two-tier), in later-stage disease only
test.w: For suspected disseminated or late Lyme disease. Not for a typical erythema migrans, which is a clinical diagnosis.
test.p: A positive EIA with confirmatory immunoblot supports the diagnosis in a compatible clinical setting.
test.n: Early serology is frequently negative because antibodies take weeks to develop. A negative result must not delay treatment of a typical expanding lesion.
test.x: Treating a typical erythema migrans on clinical grounds is the correct approach. Waiting for serology is the commonest error and it costs the patient nothing but risk.

test.l: Biopsy with direct immunofluorescence, ANA and anti-Ro/SSA
test.w: Photodistributed annular plaques, particularly with a new drug.
test.p: Interface dermatitis with a positive lupus band and anti-Ro/SSA confirms SCLE. Screen for systemic disease.
test.n: Anti-Ro is negative in a minority. Judge on histology and distribution.
test.x: Drug-induced SCLE is indistinguishable serologically and histologically. Only the medication list finds it.

test.l: Biopsy from the active border, plus fasting glucose or HbA1c
test.w: A waxy yellow atrophic plaque on the shin, and any pretibial plaque where granuloma annulare, sarcoidosis or xanthoma is a serious alternative.
test.p: Necrobiosis with palisaded granulomatous inflammation and microangiopathy confirms it. Screen for diabetes in everyone - a third have clinical diabetes and another third have abnormal glucose tolerance alone.
test.n: Normal glucose does not argue against the diagnosis; a third of cases are normoglycemic. Repeat glucose testing over time.
test.x: Biopsy the raised active border, never the atrophic yellow center. The center is burnt out, heals badly and can ulcerate. For the same reason, do not occlude these lesions.

test.l: Full mucosal examination, with HSV PCR from an active cold sore
test.w: Any targetoid eruption, before you call it minor. Examine lips, mouth, conjunctivae, genitals and anus.
test.p: Mucosal erosions make this erythema multiforme major - arrange ophthalmology review, mucosal care and admission if intake is compromised. A positive HSV PCR identifies the trigger and justifies suppressive therapy for recurrences.
test.n: A negative HSV PCR does not exclude HSV as the driver, because the eruption follows the cold sore by days to weeks. Recurrent erythema multiforme is HSV-driven until proven otherwise and is worth a suppression trial.
test.x: Targets plus mucosal erosions plus a new drug is Stevens-Johnson syndrome, not erythema multiforme major, and the management diverges completely. Count the body surface area of detachment and check the drug chart before choosing the label.

test.l: Sensory testing and nerve palpation, with slit-skin smear and biopsy for acid-fast bacilli
test.w: Any annular or hypopigmented plaque with reduced sensation, any patch that has lost hair and sweating, and any annular lesion in someone from an endemic country.
test.p: Sensory loss in the lesion, an enlarged peripheral nerve, or acid-fast bacilli establishes the diagnosis. Refer to a leprosy service, start WHO multidrug therapy and notify.
test.n: The bacterial index is low or negative in paucibacillary disease, in treated disease, and in the hands of an inexperienced technician. A negative smear does not exclude leprosy - the diagnosis is clinical plus histologic, and PCR detects early paucibacillary disease.
test.x: Nobody makes this diagnosis without testing sensation, and testing sensation takes thirty seconds. Compare pinprick, light touch and temperature inside the patch against adjacent normal skin, then palpate the ulnar, great auricular, peroneal and posterior tibial nerves.

test.l: RPR or VDRL with a confirmatory treponemal test (TPPA or FTA-ABS)
test.w: Any coppery annular or papulosquamous eruption, any eruption involving palms and soles, and any figurate erythema that does not fit. Syphilis is cheap to exclude and expensive to miss.
test.p: A reactive non-treponemal test confirmed by a treponemal test establishes it. Treat with benzathine penicillin, test for HIV, screen for other sexually transmitted infections, notify and trace partners.
test.n: Serologic tests are essentially always reactive in secondary syphilis, so a negative result in a compatible eruption should be repeated with serial dilutions before it is believed.
test.x: The prozone effect - very high antibody titers producing a falsely negative undiluted test - is the classic trap in florid secondary syphilis. Ask the laboratory to dilute the serum.

test.l: Malignancy search: history, examination, chest imaging and age-appropriate cancer screening
test.w: A rapidly migrating concentric figurate erythema, and any figurate erythema in an adult over 50 with weight loss, anemia or new constitutional symptoms.
test.p: Finding the tumor is the point. Treat it and the eruption resolves - which is itself confirmatory.
test.n: A negative first-pass workup does not close the question in a typical wood-grain eruption. Repeat imaging and keep the patient under review rather than discharging.
test.x: The commonest error is treating the rash and never looking for the cancer. The pattern itself is the indication for the search, not the presence of symptoms.

test.l: ASO or anti-DNase B titer, throat culture, ECG and echocardiography
test.s: Revised Jones criteria for acute rheumatic fever; Fitzpatrick 8e §8 Table 8-2
test.w: Evanescent non-scaling rings on the trunk of a child or young adult, particularly with fever, joint pain or a murmur.
test.p: Evidence of preceding streptococcal infection plus Jones criteria establishes acute rheumatic fever. Treat the streptococcus, refer to cardiology, and start secondary prophylaxis.
test.n: A single normal echocardiogram early does not exclude carditis - repeat it. Titers can also be normal if the pharyngitis was remote or treated.
test.x: The rings are fleeting and often absent at the moment you examine. Ask whether a rash comes and goes, and warm the skin or ask the family to photograph it - a negative examination is not a negative sign.

flag: Two bedside observations resolve most of this presentation: is there scale, and if so, is it at the edge. Scale at the edge means scrape it. No scale at all means biopsy it.
